WHY AI STOCKS ARE IMPLODING

The current implosion in so many stocks isn’t necessarily because their earnings are terrible. It’s because of how the market is reacting to and interpreting those earnings.

All of this reflects a shift in sentiment of the market participants, not some seismic shift in the fundamentals over the last few months.

The real question is whether all the stocks that were exploding higher in the spring ($INTC $SNDK $SMH $DRAM) should have been trading at those valuations in the first place.

Was sentiment far too euphoric back then? Or is the current sentiment far too bearish?

No idea and it’s not my job to know. Only time will tell.

My job is to recognize these shifts in sentiment through price action and technicals, and position myself to ride them.

Whether the market is being rational or irrational, I want to be on the right side of the move. 

I’ve been tweeting about this bearish shift in sentiment since July 2nd. July 2nd was when the $DRAM names cracked hard and broke the MA… that was the pivotal day when sentiment shifted and the euphoric trend higher in AI cracked.

First, no trader knows what’s going to happen. Everything is probabilistic at best and total noise at worst. But there are specific moments in time when the odds can become meaningfully skewed in one direction.

I personally think there's a pretty significant dislocation happening in market right now and this week gave me some of clearest evidence yet.

Both $GOOGL and $AMZN are planning to spend even more on AI infrastructure in 2027 after already investing record amounts this year with Andy Jassy even calling AI “a once in a lifetime opportunity” and making it clear Amazon has no plans to slow down.

Putting my corporate strategy hat back on I think market is overlooking something pretty important about Google because it can no longer simply decide AI is getting too expensive and go back to its traditional Search business when AI is now threatening very product that generates most of its profits.

That means infrastructure spending is becoming just as much about defending its existing business as capturing new growth which makes these investments much harder to pull back on even if investors become increasingly concerned about returns.

And that's what makes this selloff so interesting because market is punishing the companies writing the checks while those same companies are telling us they'll write even bigger ones next year.

I absolutely expect next phase of AI to become more selective with clear winners and losers but I don't think that means the infrastructure cycle is ending which is why I plan to keep adding to my highest conviction names across AI power, AI inference and Agentic AI.

quoted.text:
I went through the on-chain data on the $6.3B Binance hack. What most people are posting is WRONG, and the smartest part of this attack is getting no coverage…

The main drain took 24 SECONDS. Not 20 minutes. About $2.7B left two Binance Ethereum wallets in under half a minute.

How they got in:

Binance says a DevOps engineer's laptop "may" have been compromised. They also say there is no evidence a private key leaked. Both can be true, and that's the interesting part.

An EIP-7702 delegation needs a valid signature from the wallet. If you control a service container that is already authorised to request signatures, you never need the key. You just ask the signing service to sign for you. Same shape as Bybit, where attackers hit a developer machine at Safe.

The transaction itself:

A type-4 tx carrying 50 separate EIP-7702 authorizations, all for the Binance 14 hot wallet, all pointing at the same attacker contract.

Only ONE landed. Nonce range 18,914,775 to 18,914,824.

They didn't know the wallet's exact nonce, so they sprayed a range and let one hit. Blockaid caught this.

The part nobody is talking about:

Within 3 minutes the attacker supplied 60M USDT to Aave as collateral and borrowed 19,762 wETH against it. About $45M.

Tether froze the address right after. Aave froze the markets 46 minutes later.

TOO LATE. They had already turned freezable stablecoins into ETH nobody can touch. Marc Zeller confirmed the position is overcollateralised so Aave isn't out anything.

I traded CDS from the start in the late ’90s. Buyers were never the problem. Sellers were. 🧵

1) Banks hedged derivative counterparty risk and freed up RBC on undrawn revolvers, convert arbs hedged credit, and L/S funds went short. Long-only asset managers wouldn’t sell unless the basis was fat.

2) Synthetic CDOs fixed that. We built diversified IG CDS portfolios and got shadow ratings on the tranches. AIG FP and the ilk just wanted “high spread” for a AA or AAA. Then CDX tranching made sellers plentiful, and they were diamond hands who ignored marks. Volumes exploded. 

3) That seller died in the GFC, and CDS volumes collapsed. Now hyperscalers and chipmakers want to issue $1trn of GPU debt, and the CDS bid is massive. Who sells?

4) Asset managers should sell at a positive basis, but they haven’t yet. Pod PMs are the offer, and they aren’t diamond hands. 

Expect a thin offer side, wider spreads, and more vol.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

Philip Fisher wrote in Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits that the best companies sometimes deliberately spend heavily on future growth (research, expansion, new business lines) in ways that temporarily crush near-term earnings or cash flow.

He saw this as a feature, not a bug, provided the spending was genuine investment for the future and management had a long-range outlook.

Today’s market is doing the opposite. It is punishing Amazon, Google and Meta for turning free cash flow negative while they spend aggressively on AI infrastructure, even as these companies say this spend is a must and 2027 capex will be higher.

Fisher would have recognized this. The short-term cash burn is the cost of building capacity the companies believe will generate returns for years. The market is focused on the bill, best to focus on the opportunity.

posts.text:
Quick notes on 7702 to dispel fud and keep your funds safe.

First thing first -- 7702 itself isn't broken.  Don't panic if you are using a wallet that supports 7702 (MetaMask, Uniswap, Ambire, etc.).

To recap, 7702 is an account abstraction EIP that allows an EOA to sign a special message, called a "7702 authorization," that would insert a smart contract into the account, which enables the account to do powerful things like transaction batching, e.g. doing "approve" and "transfer" in one transaction so you can swap on Uniswap with one click.

But unfortunately the same feature also allows a hacker to efficiently move all your tokens in one single transaction.  In the Binance hack, the hacker moved ETH, USDT, and 62 other tokens in one transaction, whereas without 7702 they'd have had to send one transaction per token.  In this particular case, many of those transactions would've failed because Binance was still using the hacked wallet for withdrawals, so all transactions sent by the hacker would've had to compete with the legit transactions for nonces.  So using 7702 did help the hacker steal as much funds as possible, as quickly as possible.  Ouch!

However, in order for the hacker to use 7702, they must have either 1) had access to the private key, or 2) tricked Binance into signing a 7702 authorization.  The latter is very unlikely, as it's hard to imagine Binance being so incompetent as to expose an endpoint for signing 7702 authorizations or (even worse) for signing raw messages which the hacker could've repurposed for 7702 authorizations.  But I can't rule that out until the official postmortem.

What does all this mean for you?

- If you are a wallet developer, do NOT, under any circumstances, expose a way for third parties to request 7702 authorizations.  This is just handing your users a giant footgun to shoot themselves with.  No wallets I know of do this, so don't worry if you are a user.

- If you are a user, use a well-known wallet.  7702 does let wallet developers screw up in more ways than before, so use only well-known wallets whose developers' competence you can trust.

- If you are a company (e.g. an exchange) operating hot wallets, do NOT, under any circumstances, expose an endpoint (even if it's an internal endpoint) for signing 7702 authorizations or raw messages.

As a contributor to AA, I feel partially responsible for hacks like this, since by increasing the power of accounts, we've indeed also empowered hackers (not unlike how any new technology empowers both the good guys and the bad guys).  That said, it's important to note that 7702 was only a transitional EIP, and "endgame AA" such as Frame Transactions (EIP-8141) would allow wallet owners to set up their wallets much more securely.  For example, if Frame Transactions were available today, Binance could've:

- Set up their wallets as multisig contracts only (not EOAs).

- Set up "post conditions" for their `transfer()` functions, so that even if the multisig got hacked, the contract itself would perform sanity checks such as "no transfers of more than 1000 ETH without additional signers."

In short, the endgame of Ethereum UX is one with both optimal security and optimal UX, and users never have to trade off between the two.  But we still have a long way to go until we get there.  Back to work!

As someone who has personally spent $500k / mo+ on Google Ads for years, I can tell you with certainty: 

This revenue growth in Search is artificial & extremely unhealthy for Google’s business long term

Search volumes are declining as legacy search is being increasingly cannibalized by non-monetized LLM queries

Google’s response? 

Manufacture revenue growth via short-sighted, highly extractive, customer-hostile tactics. I.e. charge advertisers more for lower quality clicks, including clicks they do not want and explicitly did not approve Google to charge them for

A few examples to illustrate: 

For all of its history until recently, Google operated on a 2nd price auction model

I.e. if you bid $5 CPC and the next highest bidder bids $1 CPC, Google charged you $1.01 for the click (one penny more than the 2nd highest bidder) rather than the $5 you bid

This was a genius move by Google early on as it incentivizes advertisers to input their true maximum willingness to pay rather than trying to play the game of bidding low and constantly adjusting to try to stay just ahead of the next highest bidder while still not paying too much

However recently, Google silently deprecated the 2nd price auction and began charging advertisers as much as their bid and budget caps allow, regardless of what anyone else is bidding

It’s a short-sighted cash grab at the expense of the long term health of the  advertiser ecosystem

Big news, the FCC voted today to advance new satellite-to-phone rules that could benefit @SpaceX's Starlink Mobile, despite lobbying efforts by AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile to restrict parts of this proposal.

FCC: "This marks a major step to unleash American innovation and investment in next-generation connectivity."

The FCC voted to advance a proposal that would:
• Open up an additional 482 MHz of spectrum for satellite-to-phone services, expanding eligible frequency bands from 5 to 13.
• Eliminate restrictive spectrum-leasing requirements
• Remove rigid geographic coverage restrictions
• Allow more flexible agreements between satellite operators and wireless carriers
• Modernize technical rules to allow more efficient spectrum use
• Reconsider exclusive-use rights for certain satellite spectrum bands

If finalized, these changes could make it easier for SpaceX to expand Starlink Mobile, access additional spectrum, and reduce regulatory barriers.

Here's what happens next:
• Late 2026: Public comment period opens, allowing SpaceX, AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile, and others to weigh in.
• Late 2026–Early 2027: Companies submit comments and responses arguing for or against specific rule changes.
• Early–Mid 2027: The FCC reviews the feedback, evaluates interference concerns, and considers revisions.
• Sometime in 2027: The FCC holds a final vote to officially adopt the new regulations.

posts.name: Aaron Levie
posts.text:
It’s almost incomprehensible how wide the distance is between someone who’s working at the frontier with AI and basically everyone else right now. 

The crazy thing is these lines are not converging, but only growing farther apart. If the curve of AI progress had leveled off, it would certainly have given most people and companies time to catch up or implement their workflows in a standardized way. The technology would have neutralized competitive advantage because everyone would be using it the same way.

But what’s happened is the opposite. The curve of AI progress is basically going vertical right now, which means if you had codified your processes 3-6 months ago you’re likely already behind again. Now imagine most companies that kicked into gear a year ago and thought that they were done. Even further behind now.

I’ve never seen a technology in my life and career that improves at this rate, which consequently means you need to upgrade your expectations at a similar rate. Our brains weren’t wired for this, and our organizational change management processes certainly weren’t either.

With any form of recursive self improvement, things just get wilder. It’s a time when you will need to be constantly reevaluating the things that didn’t work just a couple months ago to see if they now can be solved. AI native companies certainly have a strong advantage due to this right now, so now it comes down to can the bigger companies keep up. Wild times.

And I’m sitting here thinking: *Where the hell was this in 1971? 1986? 1996? 2006? 2016?*

Meanwhile, the actual path that’s already crawling forward is the rescheduling to Schedule III. The Trump administration’s been moving that along.
